Furthermore, his method can be applied to establish local existence and uniqueness for a specific type of partial differential equation, the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, given an initial condition that is not necessarily defined at the boundary point.

A novel entity suggestion framework for Wikipedia within the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph has been developed, utilizing a unique diagram-embedding approach. This approach divides the diagram into distinct layers, with each representing various entity connection types, and employs an iterative graph algorithm to enhance entity visibility. A suggested entity is chosen by the user based on its embedded characteristics and position within the diagram. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this framework in entity suggestion, and it has been successfully deployed at Flickr.

The acceptance of kidneys from incompatible living donors would significantly increase the chances of finding a suitable donor for the growing number of end-stage renal disease patients on the transplant waiting list. However, the current protocol, which requires ideal compatibility, results in patients losing valuable time on the waiting list and occasionally passing away while waiting for a compatible kidney. We present a new concept, "ideal acceptance," which would allow the transplantation of kidneys with only 50% compatibility, reducing the waiting time and increasing the chances of finding a donor. We developed a mathematical model to analyze the benefits of ideal acceptance and estimated those benefits under various levels of compatibility. Our results suggest that ideal acceptance could decrease the waiting time by up to 90% and double the success rate of finding a compatible transplant, potentially saving up to 30% of patients on the waiting list. We also explored the economic implications of ideal acceptance from the perspective of the transplant center and patients, demonstrating that the potential gains outweigh the potential losses.

This research paper proposes an analysis framework for implicit graph connections, a recently introduced concept in the field of implicit graph models. The authors present theoretical advancements, including an expanded definition of implicit connections, a new inference algorithm named Implicit Connection Message Passing (ICMP), and a quantitative measure called Connection Preservation Ratio (CPR). These innovations enable the evaluation of implicit connections in various contexts, offering insights into the relationships between nodes with shared attributes and those without such attributes. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework by applying it to the analysis of implicit connections in two real-world datasets, Yahoo! News Groups and arXiv.

Our study examines how various word representations understand the language and
emotional context of the Loughran-McDonald text, which is frequently employed in
financial analysis to distinguish between complex and simple texts, as well as
stocks with positive and negative content. We utilize three diverse methods to
assess the embeddings: two existing classifiers and a new approach we call the
Quantitative Evaluation framework. Our evaluation framework leverages the
company-name information present in financial news articles, allowing us to
assess the embeddings' capacity to identify the emotional context of a sentence
and accurately the company being mentioned within that sentence. Using both
existing classifiers and our new framework, we find that most word representations
fail to accurately understand the emotional context of the Loughran-McDonald
text. Our analysis reveals that many of these embeddings are derived from
training data containing opposing views, thereby enabling them to recognize the
syntactic elements and polarities present in the texts but lacking a deeper
understanding of the emotional context. We also explore ways to enhance the
performances of these embeddings within the context of our evaluation framework
and discover that applying a technique called adversarial training yields
improvements in the classifications of the Loughran-McDonald text.

This article proposes a novel concept of combined power and data transfer using an OFDM system, where an integrated transmitter forms an ideal received signal for an optimal information rate at the receiver, given a power constraint and receive capabilities. A key finding is that this ideal received signal can be achieved over multiple subcarriers and using multiple transmit antennas, allowing for the maximization of both information rate and transferred power. To realize this, we develop a generalized algorithm based on convex optimization, along with a practical implementation using a SISO-OFDM equivalent framework, demonstrating a significant gain of 8.4 dB over a single-carrier system. Furthermore, we explore the potential gain provided by multiple transmit antennas and show that it can be significant in certain scenarios.

This research introduces a hybrid level-set/embedded boundary method to model the interaction of solids and fluids, applicable to problems involving phase change and advection. By representing solids as the embedded boundary of their corresponding volume of immensity, we modified the level-set technique to directly apply numerical procedures to solid particles, bypassing the need for upwind reconstruction. This approach simplifies the implementation of boundary conditions on solids for the transport equations. For problems involving phase change, we utilized an existing thin-layer Stokes solver and developed a new resolution method for the temperature equation that accounts for latent heat release. This method involves solving the temperature equation using a second-order total variation stabilization technique, resulting in a stable solution even in the presence of melt fronts. This approach was tested against both analytical and experimental data for a melting nanosphere, and produced accurate results. Furthermore, we applied our method to model the solidification of alloy metals, incorporating a Rosseland diffusion approximation to analyze related problems involving melt fronts.

Classic logical systems featuring unary operators are interpreted through functions that transform individual statements into new statements. In contrast, our approach views these operators as instructing specific transformations of the underlying language itself. In line with the principles of quantum computing, we propose that the application of an operator to a statement is analogous to the action of a gate on a qubit, with the operator's effect being a superposition of both applying to the original statement and ignoring the statement altogether. We explore how this leads to a duality between the operators and the statements they act upon, resulting in a kind of "self-duality" when an operator is applied to a particular set of statements. Our method enables the expression of increasingly complex meanings through the combination of these language-modifying operators, with a focus on capturing essential features of natural language. In addition, our system is compatible with the application of hypersequent calculi, a method for deriving valid logical statements that is both complete and sound.

We investigate a model where multiple agents, operating in a multi-agent framework, compete for optimal outcomes, with the constraint that their actions must comply with specific rationality principles. The existing literature is characterized by a focus on the binary agent model; our research is the first to explore equilibria that are based on rationalizable strategies in multi-agent systems. Our analysis reveals that it is possible to develop an learning algorithm capable of identifying rationalizable equilibria that are optimal, by leveraging the model's parameterized structure and incorporating a variety of rationality criteria. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through a series of multi-agent competition experiments, with the outcome being an optimal rationalizable equilibrium that is achieved by agents that do not have a deep understanding of game theory.

Researchers examine a model where individuals on a network share their close contacts' updated information to slow the spread of an infectious disease. This leads to a process that maps the original infection dynamics to a new gravitational system on a Euclidean plane, characterized by an exponential disease decline rate influenced by the individuals' information sharing behavior.

In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$.

A theoretical framework for adjusting PDFs has been developed, allowing for the incorporation of external datasets in addition to existing fitting protocols. The xFitter and HOLIBLEPROW framework, tailored for PDF adjustments, is based on a consistent set of equations that relate observed data to theoretical predictions, via parameters influenced by experimental uncertainties. This approach is versatile, enabling adjustments to the PDFs, as well as accessible to practitioners through a simple language, based on Python. The development of custom protocols, as well as the incorporation of additional datasets, are made possible by the flexibility of the xFitter framework.

To accelerate policy updates in reinforcement learning and compensate for missing data when sampling episodes, experience replay has been incorporated into various methods. This technique stores previously obtained data to supplement existing information when updating policy parameters. Although experience replay has been successfully integrated with policy gradient algorithms, several limitations persist in its current form. A new approach is presented in this paper that addresses these constraints by introducing a variance-reducing term in the sample policy loss function. This proposal is based on the optimal transport method and minimizes the distance between the sample distribution and target distribution. It is mathematically proven that this approach reduces the variance of the sample policy loss. The new framework is referred to as variance-reducing experience replay (V-ER). To evaluate its effectiveness, V-ER is compared to the standard experience replay method on six benchmark tasks using the DeepMind Control Suite. The results show that the proposed variance-reducing experience replay method significantly improves the performance of state-of-the-art models. The code is also openly accessible on the GITHUB platform.

libcommute/pycommute is an open-source software developed to streamline the definition and precise calculation of physical properties for one-dimensional models in condensed matter physics, utilizing a custom symbolic language for operations inspired by the principles of quantum mechanics. It distinguishes itself from traditional numerical computation tools through its robust differentiation and integration functions tailored to the parameters of Hamiltonian matrices. The software uses a unique hybrid approach, combining the efficiency of C-based matrix calculations with the symbolic manipulation capabilities of Python. The libcommute library is designed to be user-friendly, featuring intuitive function names and a comprehensive documentation that mimics the style of classic physics textbooks. The project's maintainer, J. D. Wright, is the primary developer responsible for its current iteration. The libcommute library is currently being maintained by M. A. H. Vnesud, the lead developer, who is also the first author of a study published in the Journal of Open Source Software.

We employ an experimental approach using high-resolution X-ray computed tomography to analyze the microstructure of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ superconductors at different scales.  Our findings reveal a unique combination of self-consistent electronic architecture and superconducting void configuration that promotes exceptional superconducting performance.  The inherent electronic structure, characterized by angular asymmetry and spin-polarization, is optimally maintained during the scanning process.  We demonstrate the efficacy of our method in distinguishing between different spin polarizations via angular asymmetry of the scanned sample.  Our technique allows us to map the distribution of superconducting gaps in $k$-space using scanned samples.  The results indicate the presence of a long-wavelength modulation of antiferromagnetic order that contribute to the creation of superconducting voids.  These voids are responsible for the exceptional superconducting performance by facilitating the pairing of quasiparticles via magnetic monopoles.  Our findings are corroborated by theoretical models that describe the relationship between electronic architecture, void configuration, and superconducting performance.

Both the superbosonization equation and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation serve as alternative methods for achieving bosonized descriptions in the context of supersymmetric quantum mechanics. A specific quartic superpotential is used as an example to demonstrate the application of these techniques, resulting in different types of Gaussian-like theories in both approaches. While the superbosonization equation yields a 2N-dimensional imaginary field transformation, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation leads to distinct combinations of N complex fields in various dimensions. These differences arise from distinct algebraic manipulations involving the Grassmann and bosonic variables in the two methods.

At the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the detection of the top quark's spin polarization would offer valuable insights into the heaviest fundamental particle properties, complementing existing top quark-related knowledge. This study examines the feasibility of identifying the top quark's polarization in 13 and 14 TeV proton-proton collisions, focusing on the production process involving a W boson and a light neutrino. To determine the polarization, we consider three approaches: analyzing angular correlations in decay products, searching for excess events above the predicted polarization signal, and measuring the polarization directly. This study investigates the effectiveness of these methods as a function of integrated luminosity and takes into account the influence of experimental limitations in the analysis. It finds that, despite challenges, the top quark's polarization can be determined with a certain degree of certainty in high-energy collisions. It also demonstrates that, with sufficient data, the three methods can yield accurate results, and the accuracy improves with greater luminosity. However, the polarization's precision is currently limited by theoretical predictions, and more precise calculations are needed to move forward with this analysis.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the LaNiO$_3$ metal phase using $^8$Li $\beta$-observed NMR in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our measurements consisted of gathering NMR spectra at 5.0 T and a temperature range of 20 K to 300 K for several LaAlO$_3$ bilayer counts, including 5, 10, and 20. Our results reveal that the LaAlO$_3$ spacing within the superlattices has a minimal impact on the metal phase development of LaNiO$_3$. Furthermore, our data indicate that the lattice distortion associated with the GdFeO$_3$-type distortion lessens as the LaNiO$_3$ metal phase develops, which is shown to enhance the conductivity of the LaNiO$_3$ layer. This occurs even at relatively low LaAlO$_3$ bilayer counts, where the tetravalent state of the nickel is completed prior to LaNiO$_3$ layer merging. Our findings also include local magnetic ordering and anisotropy within the LaNiO$_3$ layer, which become more pronounced as the layer thickness lessens, indicating the necessity for comprehensive study in the understanding of LaNiO$_3$ layer physics.

Current cutting-edge dialogue systems are largely categorized into two frameworks: neural network-based approaches and rule-based methods. Despite their differences, both share a common limitation - they typically cater to simple, linear scenarios found in customer service applications. In contrast, MultiTalk, a highly-branching dialogue framework, enables our system to effectively manage complex conversations with numerous possibilities, akin to topics explored on Wikipedia. This framework is characterized by numerous topic nodes, allowing our system to understand user inputs as a combination of implicit and explicit statements. To achieve this, we've developed various techniques for handling implicit meanings, such as using pre-trained language models to infer related concepts and incorporating semantic roles into our system's vocabulary. As a result, our system can engage in conversations that are not only natural but also varied, as demonstrated in our evaluation results showing our system outperforms other leading dialogue models.

Our research is centered on enhancing the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system, comprising multiple input and output antennas and a surface capable of intelligent signal reflection. To obtain an accurate calculation for this optimal capacity, we take into consideration the impact of correlated signal weakening and a more realistic method of phase shifting. A detailed analysis and corresponding metric calculation are provided for an Iris-based system, including the derivation of a key metric known as the Iris-based capacity gain. Additionally, our findings are verified through a simulation in an Iris-based system, demonstrating an average increase of approximately 8.8 decibels in maximum achievable capacity when an Iris surface is incorporated.

We've developed a new method for adapting the widely used Gadget2 simulation software to incorporate a broad class of modified gravity models, making it possible to rapidly simulate complex many-body systems while maintaining accuracy. By leveraging the algorithm's original Gadget2 heritage, we've created a seamless bridge allowing for direct comparisons between standard General Relativity-based simulations and those modified using this new method. Our approach specifically focuses on modifying the gravitational field equation using a conformal baryon field transformation, which results in a simple and computationally efficient mathematical equation when combined with a given potential energy function. When applied to multiple-body systems, this modification causes a deviation from the Newtonian law of gravity, with the difference increasing in proportion to the nth power of the system's radius, where n is a value that can be adjusted over a range from one to three. We've successfully utilized this method to simulate a variety of scenarios, including the formation of galaxy clusters, and our results show a notable improvement in performance while achieving a high degree of precision, with a speed-up of at least ten times over traditional methods for a specific example.

Miller and Sheffield established a link between the Gaussian free field and Schramm-Loewner evolution in chordal case. We extend this correlation to multiple independent SLEs driven by measures that correspond to a random free field in the unit disk, whose harmonic measure is used to drive a conformal mapping to the unit disk. We also show that multiple independent SLEs driven by measures that accumulate at Lebesgue almost sure rate on the unit circle correspond to a random free field whose harmonic measure is used to drive a conformal mapping to the unit disk.

MediaWiki-based platforms like Wikipedia and various academic projects demonstrate the effectiveness of open-source, collaborative approaches. However, developing open-source software for these types of projects remains a complex challenge. Our goal in creating WorkingWiki is to provide a modular mediawiki framework, adaptable to support independent research projects, by offering a customizable structure and robust features for plugin development.

This research investigates the interaction between a turbulent jet flame and a surrounding structure, specifically a wall that experiences vibrations due to acoustic waves produced by the flame itself. To simplify the complex problem, a method is proposed where the flame and structure are treated as two interconnected systems. The flame is modeled as a source of acoustic waves that create forced vibration in the structure, which in turn generates additional wave patterns that influence the flame. To capture this two-way interaction, the equation describing the flame's behavior includes terms representing both internal dynamics and the external force caused by the structure's vibration, induced by acoustic wave patterns. Conversely, the structure's vibration is governed by equations that take into account external force terms resulting from both the flame's internal dynamics and acoustic wave patterns. A key aspect of this research is the derivation of a linearized model for the flame and structure interaction, under the assumption that the flame's thickness is small compared to other characteristic lengths. To validate the proposed method, experimental data are analyzed for a specific test case where a methane-air flame is directed at a nearby wall that experiences acoustic wave patterns due to vibration caused by the flame's internal dynamics. Measured flame temperatures are compared with predictions made by the proposed method, both for a linearized model and the original method that includes nonlinear terms.

The study of a star's internal structure is greatly expanded by analyzing its oscillations. Seismology, the field dedicated to this study, uses vibrations to reveal a star's characteristics and understand its development. In single-component stars, standard wave types (adiabatic and Eulerian) suffice for this purpose. However, in more complex stars with multiple components, additional wave types may exist, potentially providing more valuable information. This paper explores the existence of specific wave types (convective, entropy, and Lagrangian) in polynomial-model stars with multiple components, specifically in rotating stars with convective cores and in low-mass binary stars with a compact accretor, and it outlines the potential for seismic identification of these configurations.

A new method has been proposed that can determine the existence of traveling wave chimeras and synchronized groups in networks of coupled oscillators by observing a single network variable. Once a criterion is met, a second criterion is applied to the method's results to accurately identify the locations of the synchronized groups or wave chimney within the network. Additionally, the method can be adapted to capture the dynamics of a specific system by using a specific version of the technique. To validate this method, it has been applied to a variety of networks featuring traveling wave chimeras and synchronized groups before being used to derive a new, efficient method for generating a specific type of spatiotemporal pattern.

In a two-dimensional lattice fluid with the ability to connect sites beyond nearest neighbors, we discover a unique phenomenon of clustering that reduces the entropy significantly when there are an odd number of possible connections between sites. This occurs when the number of possible connections is a prime number greater than one. To quantify this entropy reduction, we developed an entropy correction term that can be applied to the Ising model, resulting in a re-evaluation of the critical temperature under certain conditions. Moreover, our approach allows us to examine the influence of edge sharing in mean-field theories and obtains accurate results for the critical temperature when the number of possible connections is two.

Neutral current events involving neutrinos and dark matter particles may result in the breakdown of neutrino flavors, potentially causing the failure of stratospheric neutrreau decay, such as that in 0νββ decay. The influence of this phenomenon on neutrino astrophysics observations needs to be understood, so we investigate the relationship between 0νββ decay and neutrino astrophysics. We analyze how the dark matter's properties affect the probability of neutrinos interacting with it, and we present this interaction in a form that incorporates neutraurus maximum possible flavor mixing. The effect of this interaction on neutrino processes that create or destroy dark matter is calculated, with the result that it disrupts certain processes, but not others, depending on the system's energy and neutrinus characteristics. As a result, the dark matter's presence may be inferred from observations of certain systems, but it may remain undetected in others. Furthermore, we find that it has a significant impact on the production of neutrinus through the decay of dark matter, but it has a minimal effect on the production of neutrinus through the scattering of dark matter off neutrinus. Additionally, we note that it may also affect the detection of certain neutrinus, but it has no effect on the detection of others.

It has been hypothesized that extremely high-energy photons originate from distant sources above 10^19 eV, possibly originating from neutral atoms, molecules, or magnetic field structures, and could be produced by the interaction of very high-energy cosmic rays with the solar magnetic field, resulting in neutral and charged particle pairs. We examine the creation of isotropic ultra-high-energy photon flows as a result of cosmic rays interacting with the solar magnetic field, assuming that high-energy photons are produced when cosmic rays collide with magnetic field structures at the solar edge, and that pairs of neutral and charged particles are produced when photons collide with atomic nuclei at the solar core. Using mathematical models, we simulate this process and model the production of isotropic ultra-high-energy photon flows as a result of cosmic rays interacting with the solar magnetic field, and find that the predicted photon flow matches observed data, and that this prediction does not conflict with observations of cosmic rays at the solar edge.

Nonlocal gravity represents a classical modification of general relativity, influenced by the finite speed of light. This formulation modifies the Einstein field equations, adding a nonlocal term representing the gravitational effect of spatially distributed matter. A new framework for nonlocal gravity has been developed, based on constitutive connections that define the nonlocal gravitational phenomenon. These constitutive connections are determined by fundamental tetrad fields, which define the nonlocal gravitational properties of spatially distributed matter. A new approach to solving the Einstein field equations has been established, allowing for the determination of the metric and tetrad fields from nonlocal gravity's constitutive connections and the conventional Einstein field equations. A key aspect of this method involves a new fourth-order differential equation derived from nonlocal gravity's constitutive connections, along with modified Einstein field equations that can be solved using conventional techniques. This method demonstrates the nonlocal gravity effect on constitutive non-Abelian gauge fields, revealing how nonlocal gravity affects gauge fields and scalar fields. A key feature of this method is that the nonlocal gravity effect on a scalar field results in a fifth-order differential equation.

Distributed systems with multiple nodes storing and updating replicate data face a consistency challenge. To address this issue, developers implement various consistency models, but they lack a unified design framework. To bridge this gap, we propose the Eliminate-Win design framework for consistency in replicated data. This framework specifically targets conflict-free replication, covering scenarios like last-writer-wins, causal cacheability, and serializability. We've applied this design to update operations with and without keys, as well as in the presence of cacheability concerns.

To facilitate joint analysis of large datasets related to 18 human traits, researchers formed the Functional Genomic Analysis Consortium. This consortium comprised 14 institutions and made use of genome-wide association study data and functional genomic information made publicly available through the ENCODE and GWAS catalog databases. The consortium developed methods for predicting trait-associated genes, assessing genetic variation impact on trait expression and regulation, and identifying tissues and cellular processes linked to traits. These methods were applied to a broad set of traits, including diseases such as obesity, heart disease, and cancer, as well as traits like height, weight, blood pressure, cholesterol levels, blood lipid content, glucose metabolism, kidney function, sleep duration, bone density, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, colorectal cancer, obesity, inflammatory bowel disease and liver disease. The analysis revealed that multiple traits are associated with genetic variations affecting the same tissues and processes. For example, genetics affect cell cycle processes in multiple tissues, metabolism in adipose tissues, and immune cell processes in the blood. The analysis also showed that multiple traits show linkages to genetic variations affecting same tissues and processes, for example, genetics affect cell cycle processes in multiple tissues for heart disease, metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes, affect processes in immune cells in the blood for heart disease, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease and liver disease, and affect processes in cell cycle of colon for colorectal cancer, obesity and inflammatory bowel disease. The analysis further demonstrated that

This paper discusses the latest advancements made by tiny theories, including Large Extra Dimensions, Low Scale String Theory, and Brane Scenarios, within the context of the Large Hadron Collider. In addition, we examine the current experimental restrictions imposed by LHC data and its underlying underlying frameworks, specifically within the realms of composite Higgs, dark matter, and dark photons. Furthermore, we outline the prospective discoveries that could be made by the LHC, as well as the anticipated outcomes that can be derived from forthcoming experiments like ATLAS and CMS.

A notable characteristic of some neutron star binaries that emit X-rays is the consistent duration of time between their energetic bursts. Notably, a significant portion of these intervals seem to follow a specific exponential pattern. It has also been observed that some of these systems, which include the renowned Groupe des \'Etudes des Binaires \'Electromagn\'etiques (GREB) sample, exhibit this exponential distribution. However, a larger study of 132 neutron star binaries in the Galactic Centre, which includes the GREB sample as a subset, reveals that this exponential pattern is not unique to these systems. In fact, all the neutron star binaries in the study, regardless of their location, exhibit this exponential distribution. This holds true even for systems that have shown no evidence of X-ray bursts. Moreover, it is found that the curvature of these distributions, which indicates the number of bursts, varies greatly and is not solely defined by the system's inclination. This study also reveals that all the neutron star binaries in the Galactic Centre, which include both those that emit X-rays and those that do not, follow this exponential distribution. This holds true even for systems that have shown no evidence of X-ray bursts. Moreover, it is found that the curvature of these distributions, which indicates the number of bursts, varies greatly and is not solely defined by the system's inclination. This has implications for the recent discovery of a new X-ray binary in the Galactic Centre, which could either be an X-ray emitter that is

The binary system in a galaxy like our own offers unique insights into the nature of gravity.  To date, six distinct binary systems have been observed, where the two components are made up of a neutron star and a black hole, providing novel perspectives on the fundamental properties of these phenomena.  Furthermore, observations of these systems as they emit gravitational waves and other electromagnetic waves have allowed researchers to study the extreme conditions under which they form, a process that involves other factors beyond the simple collision of two objects.  These formations are a product of the complex processes involved in the creation and evolution of binary systems, influenced by factors like the movement of stars being affected by the presence of others, a process known as binary interaction.  By considering the features of these formations, researchers have been able to study the processes that create them, while also considering the effects of other factors, such as binary interaction, to a certain degree.  Nonetheless, a question still remains, given that the features of these formations are consistent with the predictions of Einstein's General Relativity, what additional information can be derived from them, a question that binary systems, particularly those composed of a neutron star and a black hole, hope to answer in the near future.

We analyzed a sample of 109 radio sources, constructed from radio maps created using data from the EVLA, taken from observations of 19 galaxies. These sources were selected based on their distance from the center of their respective galaxies and were studied in three categories: sources near the galaxy's center ($\theta_{\rm maj} \le 1.5''$), sources in the surrounding region ($1.5'' < \theta_{\rm maj} \le 5.0''$), and sources in the surrounding large region ($\theta_{\rm maj} > 5.0''$). We found radio sources with larger angular dimensions to have higher radio powers, brighter optical counterparts, and are more likely to be associated with black hole activity, whereas sources with smaller angular dimensions are more likely to be associated with neutron star activity. We also found a higher fraction of sources with larger angular dimensions showing signs of broad optical lines, and a higher fraction of sources with smaller angular dimensions showing signs of line asymmetry. However, we did not find a clear correlation between radio frequency peak and sources' angular dimensions, nor a difference in the distribution of radio core-to-jet power. We interpret these results as indicating that the jet formation process is influenced by the galaxy's central potential, particularly in the inner region.

We analyze the impact of waves generated by massive stellar explosions on the surrounding circumstellar medium, specifically SNeIb and SNeII, as well as giant eruptions of yellow hypergiants, using numerical simulations. Our goal is to investigate the generated shock waves and their interaction with the external environment, comprising smooth envelopes and molecular clouds, to better understand the phenomena of shock breakout radiation, radioactivity, and blastwaves that can produce fast-moving shocks observed in some cases. Our simulations cover the dynamic evolution of shocks in both homogeneous and inhomogeneous environments, including the disruption of dense shells, the emergence of shocks from low-density envelopes, and the interaction of shocks with molecular clouds, resulting in the production of high-velocity shocks, characterized by temperatures in the millions to tens of millions of Kelvin, and potentially producing high-energy radiation through shock-accelerated particles, as well as the acceleration of cosmic rays. We also model the detection of waves in the case of the Type II SN 2017hpa and a yellow hypergiant eruption, SMC-170908, and provide an analytical framework for the description of wave-induced shocks in external environments, emphasizing their potential to produce fast-moving shocks and associated high-energy phenomena.

This brief research extends a discovery made by Diamond--Sasaki, relating 
the geometric modularity of non-Cartan weights to arithmetic weights and vice versa 
within certain weight families, which are comprised of four-dimensional A-series weights 
whose sum of two eigenvalues equals a specific value. This value can be any integer 
from two to the highest eigenvalue, which is twenty-four. The geometric modularity of 
non-arithmetic weights in these families implies the modularity of certain non-cuspidal 
automorphic representations of GL_4 over the rationals, which are represented by an area 
on the Blake's map known as the 'diamond'. Conversely, all representations in this 'diamond' 
originate from geometric modularity of various weights within these families. This research 
also demonstrates the connection between the geometric modularity of non-arithmetic weights 
and the non-triviality of certain Hecke algebras at prime powers, which are used as an additional 
tool in identifying the modularity of these representations and weights.

Quantum interactions between a particle's spin, vibration, and position are more than just classical notions. This concept is not limited to spatial variations but can also be influenced by momentum, potentially leading to a more comprehensive understanding of quantum phenomena. In this study, we incorporate a harmonic oscillation into the one-dimensional spin-orbit coupling model and investigate the effects of momentum on electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational interactions. Our findings show increased stability in vibrational states due to the quantum competition between the electron-vibrational interaction and the spin-vibrational one. Additionally, we identify a quantum phenomenon where the electron-vibrational interaction can switch between two different modes by adjusting the vibrational frequency. This may provide a foundation for exploiting quantum effects in stabilize energy levels within potential energy landscapes.

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approachable introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack in the existing literature by bringing together key results from the field in a comprehensive overview.

Researchers incorporate diverse semantic representations to enhance their models' understanding of language. Different frameworks such as Compositional Vector Semantics, Neural Network-based Inference, and Graph-based Semantics coexist to cover various aspects of natural language. This paper explores the benefits of using multiple semantic frameworks in a disciplined way. It establishes a robust evaluation framework to assess the individual strengths and weaknesses of various semantic models. Our evaluation reveals that distinct models excel in different NLI tasks, with some models performing exceptionally well on specific categories. Notably, the performance of these models varies significantly when they are tested on different categories. Our study's findings suggest that there is considerable variety in the semantic of natural language, making it challenging for a single model to achieve outstanding results across all types of discourse. As a result, it is difficult to evaluate the models' understanding of language solely by applying them to natural language tasks. Consequently, our evaluation framework includes a second set of tests that assess the models' ability to capture the semantic of natural language from different perspectives. All of our data and the evaluation framework are available for download at https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/2021.acl-short-abstracts#paper_3.

Automated driving systems depend on predictive safety modules to assess risks and avoid accidents. However, developing reliable risk prediction models is challenging due to the necessity for extensive and diverse data sets, combined with difficulties in validating their effectiveness. This study focuses on detecting high-risk situations during lane changes, a critical maneuver. It utilizes a unique data set containing lane change video snippets with associated risk labels, and employs a semi-supervised approach to build and test a deep learning model. The data set's limited annotation information is utilized to train a lane detection algorithm, enabling the model to utilize pre-trained network weights. This allows the model to operate independently of specific annotated data, and is tested using a diverse test set to evaluate its performance. The research reveals that a deep spatiotemporal learning network is an effective method for detecting hazardous lane changes, and that the model's ability to analyze both local and global video patterns is crucial. Additionally, the study shows that the proposed model's performance is largely unaffected by lane detection accuracy.

The prevailing theory that large, fast-spinning objects must lose mass to complete rotation is not universally accepted. Using numerical simulation, we have modeled objects with masses below 0.08 solar masses that are composed of multiple layers, including a solid core, surrounded by a layer of hydrogen and helium gases, and an outer atmosphere. We have calculated their rotation periods, assuming they have solidified in place. Our key findings include: objects with masses above 0.06 solar masses can achieve equilibrium through mass loss; below this threshold, they can already spin at required speeds without shedding mass; we have determined the specific conditions under which objects can lose mass; and, our results are consistent with observations of rapidly rotating brown dwarfs. Furthermore, we have found that objects with masses below 0.05 solar masses may have distinct internal structures comprising a solid core surrounded by a liquid-metal hydrogen layer. This unique structure may influence their magnetic field generation and overall behavior.

The amplitude assessment technique, widely used in seismic hazard and risk research, involves a significant number of variables that are typically treated as random for computational efficiency. It is not uncommon for hundreds to over a thousand such variables to be incorporated into the method, with their impacts often difficult to quantify or cannot be modeled precisely. The inherent complexity arises from the fact that each contributing factor has a distinct effect on the outcome, making it challenging to accurately depict their collective impact through a straightforward formulation. The main obstacle lies in accurately capturing the statistical distribution of the amplitude when modeling the interaction of so many variables, particularly considering that each factor has a unique influence on the outcome. The proposed stochastic simulation method aims to overcome this challenge by breaking down the amplitude assessment process into a series of interconnected stochastic steps, allowing for a more realistic depiction of the effects of variables on the amplitude through a combination of deterministic and stochastic components. The new approach is expected to yield a more accurate statistical distribution of the amplitude, which is essential for conducting robust risk computations. The developers of the method are encouraged to share their assessment processes, enabling the creation of a realistic depiction of the impacts of variables on the amplitude, thus facilitating a more accurate statistical distribution that is vital for risk computations.

A new comprehensive framework has been developed to model a broad category of relativistic afterglows, specifically those that occur following a gamma-ray burst. This framework, based on a universal expression for radiative energy, generates a dynamic relationship between radiative and non-radiative components. It results in a singular equation that encapsulates the intricate dynamics of afterglows, eliminating the need for distinct phases and transitions. Furthermore, this single equation facilitates the prediction of afterglows in various contexts, including interactions with external mediums and relativistic shock waves. It also provides a framework for examining the afterglow's extreme relativistic phase and offers a new perspective on the dynamics of gamma-ray bursts in dense environments.

Bipartite graph vertex partitioning problems have been extensively studied, in which two sets of nodes are distinct and separate, representing different entities, and an edge connects two nodes if they represent the same entity. The Bipartite Vertex Separation Problem aims to divide the nodes of one set into the fewest possible subsets, such that the nodes of the other set remain separate. We have developed a new algorithm for solving this problem exactly, using a fixed parameter, being the number of subsets in one of the sets. Conversely, research has shown that the problem does not have a fixed parameter tractable (FPT) solution for a single subset. We have also established FPT algorithms for specific variant problems, including finding the minimum number of subsets required to separate a specific set of nodes, and determining if a given subset of nodes can be separated from the remaining nodes.

Deep neural network algorithms have achieved high accuracy in image classification tasks, but can struggle with incremental learning tasks due to their susceptibility to data dominance. This limitation is exacerbated when the training data evolves over time with the addition of new classes, a process known as incremental learning with new classes. This paper explores several techniques for addressing this challenge, including weight calibration, data re-balancing, and learning rate optimization. It introduces three innovative methods for addressing imbalanced incremental learning with new classes, including the dynamic average method, the calibration network, and the adaptive re-balancing factor method. It also proposes a comprehensive evaluation framework consisting of 6000 randomly selected images from 20 categories of the CIFAR-100 dataset. This dataset is further divided into five independent test datasets to ensure the results are robust and reliable. It conducts a thorough comparison of the proposed methods with five alternative techniques, resulting in the discovery of two techniques that consistently outperform the others. It also finds that the best method varies depending on the dataset, but interestingly, one technique tends to perform better than the others on certain datasets.

Current robotic bipedal locomotion systems rely heavily on powerful actuators to achieve stable, efficient, and resilient gait. However, the risk of actuator burnout and walking instability remains a significant challenge. To address this issue, we are investigating the integration of propellers into robotic legs to create a hybrid system that leverages both leg-based and air-based propulsion methods. This hybrid approach aims to reduce the burden on actuators during certain phases of the walking cycle, potentially leading to enhanced resilience, stability, and bipedal efficiency. This paper presents our initial concept, modeling a human-inspired gait where propellers facilitate backward movement, and includes theoretical and simulated data to support our hypothesis. Further research and testing are needed to validate the benefits of this hybrid approach in a realistic, human-scale bipedal setting.

Let $k$ be an infinite perfect field, considered as a component of the field $K$, which also includes the field of rational functions $\overline{k}$ over $k$. Noting that $\overline{k}$ equates to the algebraic closure of $k$, we designate $\overline{k}$ as the composite field of $K$. Furthermore, we define a map $\phi$, which, for each place $v$ in the field of rational functions $\overline{K}$, determines a corresponding place $w$ in the field $k$. Under the assumption that the map $\phi$ is a resolute map, particularly one that is surjective, we aim to demonstrate the following conclusion: given any finite set of places $\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_d\}$ in the field of rational functions $\overline{K}$, with corresponding places $\{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_d\}$ in the field $k$, there exists a field $L$, which is an extension of the field $k$, such that the restriction of the map $\phi$ to the set of places $\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_d\}$ in the field of rational functions $\overline{L}$ is surjective.

Recent research aiming to minimize CPU energy consumption during secure encryption tasks proposed using side-channel attacks that trigger specific CPU events, which are then used to introduce errors in the encryption output. However, implementing these techniques at high speeds is challenging. To address this issue, our research introduces HyperDegrade, a novel approach that combines two techniques - Hyper-Threading and thread degradation - to enhance encryption speed efficiency. When executed on a system with Hyper-Threading enabled, HyperDegrade takes advantage of the existing infrastructure with minimal modification, but it yields a 5x improvement in encryption speed,, whereas, on systems without Hyper-Threading, it achieves a 2x improvement. Moreover, our research demonstrates that HyperDegrade's attack-and-degrade strategy can be applied to a variety of cryptographic functions like AES, RSA, and ECDSA, resulting in a 5x, 2x, and 2x improvement in encryption, key generation, and digital signature creation, respectively.

To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts with other fields in a manner that involves dimension-six operators. Based on the combined constraints from the $B$-anomalies and electroweak precision data, we found that the Higgs's contribution to the muon's magnetic moment anomaly could amount to as much as $8.3\sigma$ (or $4.4\sigma)$ standard deviations, contingent on whether the Higgs interacts with a heavy neutral sector in a manner that respects the $SU(3)_\text{QED}$ symmetry. Alternatively, if the Higgs interacts with a light effective operator, its contribution to the anomaly would stand at $5.5\sigma$ standard deviations. Moreover, our analysis demonstrates that forthcoming experiments at the Large Hadron Collider such as LHCb and NA62 can either confirm or rule out the Higgs's contribution to the anomaly by a margin of several standard deviations, assuming the Higgs's contribution to the anomaly is as large as expected.

The investigation focuses on the decay of heavy neutral bosons to quarks plus photons, considering all relevant combinations of couplings and taking into account the internal structure of hadrons via lattice QCD. It also examines radiative decay modes of mesons, specifically D and B mesons, as well as the heavy neutral boson X(2234A). It utilizes data from the lattice threshold ratios of the decay widths to the masses of the hadrons, and for the X boson, it utilizes experimental cross-section data. For the X boson, the study finds the mass to be 2234. MeV with an uncertainty of 13.5, the decay width to be 26. MeV with an uncertainty of 10.6, and the coupling to be 0.625 with an uncertainty of 0.083, and for the D meson, the decay width is found to be 102. MeV with an uncertainty of 0.4, and for the B meson, the decay width is found to be 18.5 MeV with an uncertainty of 0.4. It also includes an estimate for the decay width of the $\tau$ lepton.

A novel, straightforward algorithm has been developed for identifying whether a given link is knotted or unknotted. This method, tailored for traditional and welded links, utilizes a novel, unsymmetric cross-section of the link to determine if it is possible to transform the link into an unknotted state without breaking any of the curve's segments. A key advantage of this approach is that it allows for the use of local improvements to the link's configuration during the unknotting process. As a result, this algorithm can be used to define a distance metric between knotted links, with the potential to develop a specialized algorithm for determining if two links are identical.

Given a finite number of rational functions in one variable over a semifield K, denoted as f_i(x), we can construct a tropical curve C by defining its points as the solutions (x_0, x_1,..., x_n) that make the inequalities \sum_{i=0}^{n} \nu(f_i(x_0,x_1,...,x_n)) \geq 0 and the inequality \sum_{i=0}^{n} x_i hold true, along with the requirement that local coordinates exist on the connected components of C. We can then establish a logarithmic semifield of rational functions, denoted as k(C), on the tropical curve C by using the valuation map \nu: k(x_0,x_1,...,x_n) \to \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}. Our research shows that the semifield k(C) is finitely generated as an semifield over its base semifield K.

This paper introduces a specific Vassiliev invariant, denoted as $\tau$, which is linked to the Fox-Hatcher 1-cocycle of the pure braid group associated with the monoid of rooted trees. Specifically, $\tau$ is a non-trivial, order-three Vassiliev invariant that derives its name from its connection to the Fox-Hatcher 1-cocycle. Moreover, we establish in this paper that $\tau$ is an invariant that is distinct from other known Vassiliev invariants of order three, though it does share a multiplicative property in common with one of them. We also find that $\tau$ exhibits specific values in relation to the braid group's central elements and its torus subgroup, thereby providing further insight into its nature.

New analysis from the KATRIN experiment provides significant constraints on electron anti-neutrino masses, with lower bounds of 0.11 eV for a standard neutrino model and 0.18 eV in models requiring additional sterile neutrino phases. These constraints significantly impact lower mass limits for neutrino masses generally, with 0.19 eV as the standard minimum and 0.30 eV in the presence of additional sterile phases.

Nesta apresentação, exploraremos as técnicas de multiplicação de matrizes, discutiremos as desvantagens dessas abordagens e examinaremos as diferenças entre a execução sequencial no processador e a execução paralela na unidade de processamento gráfico.

In cooperative tasks, robots with agent functionality can collaborate and exchange information to achieve common goals more effectively. To facilitate this cooperation, a collaborative communication network is established among the robots. Considering the limitations of the robots' computational and communication capabilities, we develop a communication strategy that minimizes data exchange while optimizing the objective function of an overall coactivation problem. A robust algorithm is presented to determine the optimal strategy by exchanging limited information, and it is shown that the proposed strategy meets the computational and communication constraints of the robots. Furthermore, the efficiency of the algorithm is evaluated in a scenario where a group of robots must cover a moving target.

As precision strategies mature for future colliders like the HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and CPPC, accurately controlling theoretical predictions becomes essential. We've integrated IR effects into the amplitude-driven resummation approach, offering a unified framework that's expected to provide the leading logarithmic accuracy in final-state and/or infrared divergent parts. This expectation is grounded in the impact of threshold and soft logarithms, specifically in massive processes like top quark production, where the accuracy might be limited by logarithmic enhancements associated with the $m_T$ scaling. Although remarkable progress has been made, several challenges remain in the field, including the handling of non-global logarithms, running couplings, and heavy particle masses, particularly in cases where the mass exceeds the cutoff.

As the concept of federated learning evolves, so does its application in the education sector, particularly in a vertical setting where schools and institutions train models together to address social issues. However, this setup also creates opportunities for a type of attack known as a pragmatic privacy assault, where the attacking institution sends misleading data to the learning process. This paper explores this type of attack in the context of vertical federated education and investigates its effectiveness, as well as possible defense mechanisms, to better understand how to secure FL-based educational applications.

Kernel-based methods, particularly those like Support Vector Machines, are effectively utilized due to their global optimization nature and ability to handle complex data sets. However, constructing an optimal kernel depends on determining the reproductive coherent measure, which can be challenging, especially with limited data. A novel approach is proposed to estimate the kernel based on data, involving the use of random Fourier features as pseudo measurements, and formulating a maximum likelihood estimator to optimize kernel parameters. Rather than treating the data as independent identically distributed, the proposed method leverages the unique characteristics of Fourier features to develop an efficient estimator, which significantly reduces the computational complexity compared to traditional non-iterative estimators. The method is evaluated on multiple classification and clustering datasets, demonstrating its computational efficiency and effectiveness.

The study offers a novel approach to embedding groups into product spaces known as Garland spaces, specifically tailored for groups with a Cartesian decomposition structure. The method provides a clear, systematic framework for generating a minimal set of generators for these product spaces. Additionally, the paper presents an efficient algorithm to compute the fundamental group of these product spaces, yielding significant computational benefits when compared to conventional methods.

This research paper examines a specific conformal invariant, called M\"obius curvature, on the surface of a hypersphere in dimension $n+2$. We demonstrate that M\"obius curvature cannot be modified by changing the surface's position or orientation. In other words, if a surface has the same shape as another surface in the same hypersphere, but is located or oriented differently, then its M\"obius curvature will be the same as the first surface's M\"obius curvature. This concept is unique to M\"obius curvature, as we show that it does not apply to other types of curvature, such as Ricci or Gauss curvature, especially when the surface is not a great circle. Our proof relies on techniques related to conformal mapping and the use of the Jacobi operator to analyze the surface's properties.

Optimally timing surgical interventions for transitioning cardiac tissues in congenital heart defect patients requires precise pre-operative analysis. Currently, this process relies heavily on manual cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) image segmentation, which is both time-consuming and prone to human error. To automate this process, a study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of a trained UNet network in accurately identifying left ventricular mass in patients with one specific type of heart defect (Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome). To increase the limited availability of training data, techniques such as data augmentation were used. The research compared the results of a trained model against those obtained from human operators who had previously segmented the same images, with an emphasis on assessing the level of precision and speed. It was found that the UNet network was not only significantly faster at completing the task but also achieved a more accurate measurement. Although some variation existed, the study showed that the automated system was reliable and consistent in its calculations, with a high correlation to the human-derived data. Furthermore, the research highlighted the potential for a much broader application of automated CMR image analysis across various types of congenital heart defects.

This research focuses on a linear model that makes predictions for the rate of deformation and stress within various materials, particularly plastic solids, fractures in brittle materials, and elastoplastic substances with stick-slip behavior. A generalized model that incorporates properties of all these materials has been developed, and its underlying principles have been explained in terms of the mathematics of partial differential equations. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the model has been applied to a specific problem involving the slip of elastoplastic fluids over inclined planes; it yielded a solution that shows the model's ability to capture the experimentally observed static friction coefficient, and also predicts the onset of stick-slip behavior under specific conditions.

A new framework for a multi-service wireless system that employs SWIPT is presented, considering an energy-harvesting receiver and various services with different requirements. The system model utilizes a non-orthogonal multiple access technique and forms an optimization problem to maximize overall system performance by maximizing harvested energy and meeting each service's demand. To solve this problem, an algorithm is developed that utilizes quasi-maximum filtering and reduces computational costs, and simulations compare its effectiveness.

Our proposed technique, known as MultiItem Examination (MIX), tackles the challenging problem of examining multiple items from a single glance. This involves selecting the most pertinent items from a vast array of options, perhaps arranged in a grid or a table. Our primary innovation is a method that uses inter-item interactions to determine the best items to analyze, where our secondary contribution is a simple replacement for existing attention-based techniques. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach at detecting important code elements in a visual code editor and identifying crucial objects in a video game, achieving superior results to existing models in both cases.

Complex, multi-factorial datasets are increasingly being analyzed with Bayesian conditional models, due to their ability to handle large datasets and incorporate prior knowledge. However, despite their utility, these models can generate artificial extremes in the data, surpassing the real data limits, which can be misleading and affect subsequent analyses. For example, artificial extremes can influence the development of new predictive models and distort statistical estimates of rare events. Our research addresses this issue by providing an upper limit for the real data distribution, while retaining the original data probabilities for realistic extremes. This limit is derived from a Bayesian conditional model, using the posterior distribution of the data's generating parameter, and is referred to as the 'Extreme Conditional Upper Bound'. Our method is applicable to any Bayesian conditional model and is suitable for large datasets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in controlling the overestimation of rare events and provide a suitable metric for evaluating the artificial extremes generated by these models. Furthermore, we explore the limitations of our approach, the potential for artificial limits to occur and the advantages of using our method over alternative methods.

This paper focuses on releasing a set of data used for testing the understanding of language, specifically targeted at resolving word ambiguities. We began by examining previously employed methods for Term Sense Disambiguation, then developed an alternative approach, which is now presented as Huang et al.'s GlossBERT model. This new approach is part of a comprehensive system for solving the TSD task, and is known as the Huang et al. GlossBERT system. The dataset we created to evaluate the effectiveness of this approach is now made available to the research community. It is called the Huang et al. GlossBERT system.

In complex systems like hospitals, understanding how procedures are carried out requires more than just seeing the final process - it also demands an insight into the underlying processes and their interconnections. Currently available machine learning approaches can describe individual steps in the process, but cannot capture the underlying processes and relationships between the steps. Our research introduces the concept of capturing complex procedures through multimodal documents that combine text and graphs, and develops two novel evaluation metrics that measure the understanding of expert procedures through two aspects: the processes and the relationships between the steps. We tested our approach in two domains, surgery and chemical synthesis, and found that it outperformed the existing single-modal methods in both domains.

In the early stages of a random graph system, particularly during the explosive growth phase, the graph's structure undergos a significant transformation as it transitions from a tree-like architecture to a highly connected, random graph. This critical period is marked by the emergence of a power-law distribution in the sizes of subgraphs generated by an edge in the underlying network. Our research focuses on an unbounded distribution where the subgraphs formed by following random edges in the underlying network represent a prime example of a scale-free distribution. It has previously been demonstrated that a random graph based on a fundamental operation exhibits explosive growth and a power-law distribution in the sizes of subgraphs generated by an edge. However, the existence of a scale-free distribution in random graphs based on the same operation during their explosive growth phase remains an open question. This research confirms that the Cayley graph's edge distribution does indeed exhibit a prime example of a scale-free distribution in its explosive growth phase.

A fundamental question in probability remains unresolved: is the characteristic polynomial of a random unitary matrix universal, sharing core properties with a specific family of polynomials called Airy polynomials? To address this, our research focuses on an expanded version of the polynomial, called universal Airy polynomials, which capture the essential features of the characteristic polynomial's asymptotes as they relate to the NIVPE problem. Leveraging connections between the characteristic polynomial and the NIVPE process, as well as the Airy process, we established upper and lower bounds for the probability of NIVPE events in terms of universal Airy polynomials. These results provide strong evidence that the characteristic polynomial's asymptotic behavior can be represented by the universal Airy polynomials, offering a powerful analytical tool. Furthermore, our approach enables the derivation of refined estimates for NIVPE probabilities, revealing the probability's asymptotic behavior as it approaches zero is governed by a specific exponent, currently unknown. We also explored connections between the universal Airy polynomials and another important object, the type-A Cauchy process, establishing a direct relationship between them.

Our proposal aims to address the challenge of achieving high-frequency responsiveness in gravitational wave sensors. We suggest a novel sensor design called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which incorporates a fluid cavity to increase its sensitivity while reducing the need for massive mirrors. This design leverages the unique properties of a fluid cavity to enhance its resonance at specific frequencies, allowing for higher-frequency detection. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this design, we model its response to a simulated gravitational wave signal and compare it to a conventional Sagnac interferometer, showing that the sloshing Sagnac design can achieve a higher signal-to-noise ratio at higher frequencies. Furthermore, we explore various parameters that can optimize the sensor's performance and consider the potential applications and future developments of this design.

A key performance driver for Large-Scale MIMO (LS-MIMO) systems is their ability to adopt a compact cell size, enabling higher spectral and spatial efficiency. However, this capability may compromise LS-MIMO's effectiveness in dense urban environments due to increased interference and reduced signal-to-noise ratio. As a result, researchers have been exploring a versatile LS-MIMO system design, referred to as Extra Large MIMO (XL-MIMO), which combines the advantages of small cells and large spatial dimensions. A novel XL-MIMO system design, called XL-MIMO Stochastic Access Protocol (XSAP), has been proposed to tackle the challenge of managing complex spatial interference. In XSAP, each XL-MIMO base station independently makes decisions regarding uplink transmission, utilizing random threshold values. These decisions are based on whether the base station detects signal transmission from a specific location, defining a stochastic boundary around which visibility areas do not overlap. A key performance metric of XSAP, referred to as non-intersecting visibility area probability (NIP), has not been previously analyzed due to the absence of a suitable probabilistic model. This paper presents a first probabilistic model for NIP, which provides a framework for evaluating XSAP's performance. In addition, the paper presents various NIP analytical results, along with corresponding numerical validation, to provide insights into the XSAP protocol's behavior and potential for optimizing transmission probabilities to maximize non-overlapping visibility areas.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have significantly enhanced our understanding of young star-forming regions' properties. However, the vertical perspective has often been neglected in such observations. A previous study demonstrated that disk instability causes spiral patterns and knots in the gas and dust of young star-forming regions around a specific mass range. It also highlighted the importance of considering disk structure and dynamics in the analysis of such regions. The aim of this study is to determine the observable consequences of disk structures and dynamics in the dust continuum under specific radiative transfer conditions. It focuses on the vertical shear instability's effects on disk structures and dynamics. The model used in this study involves a radiative transfer simulation utilizing the vertical shear instability's model for disk structures and dynamics. It incorporates the effects of optical thickness, temperature, and gas-dust coupling. The model simulation produces features such as spiral arms, knots, and ring-like structures in the dust continuum. These features are largely independent of the optical thickness and gas-dust coupling parameters. They are, however, significantly affected by the temperature model, especially in the ring-like structure formation. Two examples of young star-forming regions, LLauri and L1489, are used to determine the limitations of this study's model. The model's results match the observed features in these regions. It is also found that the magnetic field strength required by the vertical shear instability model is within the observable limit in L1489. However, it is beyond the limit in

The term "Big Apple strength" is used to describe the unique distribution of angular momentum within the spectrum of the harmonic oscillator potential. A mathematical framework "strength" is a measure of how significantly the potential is modified. Calculations are undertaken for a harmonic oscillator potential in three dimensions with an added central four-body interaction, which results in Big Apple strength. The added interaction causes the usual rotational symmetry to be modified, leading to a more complex spectrum. Consequently, the coupling between different orbital angular momentum states is altered, affecting the relative energies of different band structures. Theoretical models such as the harmonic oscillator shell model can benefit from this complexity to better align with experimental data, particularly for particles like omega and phi mesons. The concept of Big Apple strength may also be relevant to the study of astronomical objects like neutron stars and white dwarfs, which are known to spin rapidly due to their small size. The relationship between strength and the objects' spin rate is explored, which leads to the proposal of a new metric called spin rate parameter that can distinguish between a neutron star and a white dwarf.

Using a first-principles DMFT approach on a simplified model, we analyzed the impact of correlated electrons in perovskite compounds, specifically examining the effects of hybridization and atomic properties in SrMnO$_3$. A line of studies was conducted under constant energy conditions, applying DMFT methods to a simplified model derived from DFT, with parameters adjusted to match experimental frequencies, charges, and orbital occupations. Our results show that the complexity of perovskite electronic structures can be understood through simplified models, demonstrating the significance of correlated electron interactions in determining orbital sequences. Our approach also highlighted the importance of hybridization in determining the magnetic exchange interaction, with estimates ranging from -400 to -600 meV, influenced by the choice of model and exchange pathway. Our research suggests that the one-electron spectrum should be analyzed from multiple perspectives, emphasizing the need for careful model construction to avoid artificial orbital crossings.

This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent motional frequency. To begin, balanced multi-modal motivation is used to establish a harmonic oscillator that resists frequency changes, critical for the molecular quantum gate. Next, two long quantum registers are generated from the motivated ions, with operations performed on the harmonic oscillator frequency to control the gate's efficacy. Finally, the harmonic oscillator frequency is modified to separate the quantum registers, allowing the execution of frequency-changing Molmer-Sorensen gates for two-dimensionally coupled quantum computations.

Using advanced spectroscopic techniques, researchers previously identified that paraelectric KTaO3 and SrTiO3 have local polarizations around titanium and tantalum ions. This study delves into structural data from X-ray diffraction and provides a more detailed examination of atomic positions. By applying a precise method to measure polarization, the study demonstrates that local polarizations in these materials are indeed greater than expected, ranging from 0.45e to 0.86e, and are directly proportional to the electric susceptibility measured through dielectric constants. Furthermore, the study reveals that these polarizations vary significantly across different titanium/tantalum site environments, correlating with vibrational modes and enabling the interpretation of lattice anomalies in dielectric measurements.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on lattice distortions that lead to strong spin-orbit coupling and unusual topological properties in 5d transition metals. A particular class of materials exhibits both strong spin-orbit coupling and strong spin interactions due to their unusual electronic structure and geometric arrangement. These characteristics suggest that these materials may harbor exotic states of matter, such as magnetic topological insulators and superconductors, particularly those with fermion pairings linked to both strain and orbital interactions. However, the underlying physics that drives their unusual properties in these materials remains poorly understood. Here, a fundamental theoretical framework has been developed to describe the unusual physics associated with these materials entering the strong coupling regime. This framework involves a multivalued surface in the parameter space, characterized by a triadic relationship between strain, orbital effects, and superconductivity. We used this framework to predict that straining h-Bi$_2$Se$_3$ will enter a strong Dirac metal state, characterized by robust surface states resistant to backscattering, and will also predict other materials that will enter this state upon strong tension. Additionally, we used advanced computational techniques to confirm that the predicted state of matter in tense h-Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is a strongly linked Dirac metal that exhibits surface states at all energies, and will also enter a superconducting state upon application of a magnetic field.

This paper introduces a new mathematical framework that enables the derivation of various frequency and ratio measures used in statistics and data analysis. It establishes an underlying structure and formulates the Skewness and Kurtosis coefficients used for a distribution's fourth moment. Furthermore, it demonstrates the creation of novel frequency and ratio measures by manipulating this structure. The paper's techniques are applied to skewness and kurtosis measures, resulting in derivations that are both intuitive and accessible. The paper's authors propose the term "bimomb" to describe objects defined by this new mathematical framework.

We investigated the production of neutral leptons in the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, utilizing a hadronic neutrino production mechanism commonly seen in weak interactions. By analyzing this reaction at the NA62 experiment, we determined the significant potential of NA62 to greatly expand our understanding of a fundamental neutrino parameter, the mixing parameter between a neutral lepton and a muon, within the range of $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-11}$. This could reveal neutral lepton masses as small as $O(10^{-12})$ eV, enabling insights into the lepton unitarity problem or potential neutrino losses in the universe. NA62 can also slightly improve current limits on a neutral lepton decay constant into one nucleon, potentially bearing implications for matter-antimatter asymmetry.

In a Galilean frame, light waves travel at a speed of $c$ in a vacuum.
