A cutting-edge accelerator with high-energy muons and ions has immense potential to drive groundbreaking advancements in several fields, including particle physics, nuclear physics, and materials science. By leveraging the unique properties of muons and the strength of the muon-nucleus interaction, this accelerator could significantly enhance our understanding of muon physics. Furthermore, it would enable the exploration of nucleus structure at the TeV scale, revealing hidden aspects of nuclear physics. Moreover, a muon-ion accelerator could develop the world's most precise sources of muon beams, enabling innovative searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model. To explore the feasibility and potential of this accelerator concept, we propose developing a prototype accelerator that could pave the way for the realization of this visionary project.

A novel approach is proposed to create respiratory-motion-adjusted 4D T2-weighted MRI images, suitable for whole-body imaging, by combining a unique data acquisition method with a refined image reconstruction process. The proposed technique leverages a data acquisition strategy that adjusts for respiratory variations during scanning, ensuring consistent imaging positioning, combined with a refined reconstruction process to produce high-quality 4D MRI images from acquired data. The technique's performance was evaluated by comparing its results with those from a conventional 4D MRI technique, using both numerical simulations and actual subject scans as test data. The study demonstrated that the proposed technique yields 4D MRI images with better spatial resolution, snakelike structure resolution, and overall image clarity, compared to conventional 4D MRI. Furthermore, the study found that the proposed technique's performance is comparable to that of a highly optimized conventional 4D MRI technique, in terms of resolution and image clarity, while offering the advantages of free-breathing scanning, reduced scan time, and elimination of the external respiratory sensor, making it more comfortable and efficient for lengthy whole-body MRI scans.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to achieving secure control in complex cyberphysical systems by utilizing Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) that are constrained in their input requirements. It begins by establishing a general framework for defining and utilizing Discrete Control Barrier Functions (DCBFs) in systems with continuous and discrete dynamics. A core component of this framework involves determining the optimal security-invariant control strategy by solving a linear programming problem, which is feasible if a specified set containing the system's initial state has a discrete trajectory reaching the safety criterion defined by the CBFs. Additionally, the paper explores the robust execution of CBF-based control by accounting for unknown cyber attacks, involving the resolution of a convex optimization problem to determine a safety-preserving control input, which can be achieved through the application of a fast security monitoring and mitigation framework. Key benefits of this approach include the ability to efficiently handle a wide range of state dimensions, facilitate the implementation of learning-based secure control through the incorporation of a monitoring and mitigation framework, which enables the quick recovery of systems following cyber attacks, resulting in minimal impact on system performance.

Geometric regions can be distinguished by various attributes such as boundary type, orientation, orientation after differentiation, and CF-approximation areas. This research explores the potential of combining these characteristics to identify distinct regions. Our analysis reveals that only a limited set of combinations yields unique attributes, consisting of the combination of a boundary type and a orientation type. Therefore, we define a new concept, CF-approximation area combination, to describe unique geometric regions. This research also introduces the concept of a function being CF-admissible in a region, defined as its ability to produce the same CF-approximation area combination when differentiated. We demonstrate that CF-admissible functions share the same attribute with the original function, a property that holds for both approximate and exact areas, as well as the underlying region's boundary type and orientation type. This research paves the way for the creation of new mathematical theories on geometric regions and their associated functions.

The paired-permutation examination is a recently suggested statistical method for validating the integrity of software test cases, specifically designed to identify potential discrepancies between actual results and expected outcomes generated by test cases. This paper proposes the adoption of accurate paired-permutation examination as a reliable test metric in software development, capable of ensuring test cases are effective and efficient.

This dataset contains historical information on freight costs, shipping volumes, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrap ship values from 1966 to 2020, enabling research into freight cost drivers, shipping industry dynamics, and the unique economics of the cargo shipping sector.

Geometric quantization relies heavily on symplectic reduction, yet this technique often yields reduced spaces with non-standard geometric properties, making them unsuitable for conventional quantum field theory applications. Recent studies have utilized algebraic geometry to analyze reduced spaces, specifically to quantify their classical limits, but the resulting approach falls short in addressing crucial quantum geometry aspects. In contrast, our proposed 'fabric spaces' framework involves reduced geometric quantization and a broad generalization of algebraic geometry's Duflo-Mackay formula, allowing us to pinpoint the classical limit and identify key geometric properties of a quantum field theory. To demonstrate its utility, we use fabric spaces to show that certain reduced spaces have triangulations that diverge in the limit, implying a broken Lorentz invariance in the corresponding quantum field theory. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the generalization of divergent triangulations to matrix quantum gravity.

Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple classification tasks using graphical data, albeit frequently employing thousands of parameters. Our novel approach, which combines graph pruning and simplification, successfully reduces the parameters of these models to a mere hundred while maintaining their accuracy. By systematically removing nodes and edges from complex graphs, our method bypasses the limitations of arbitrary metric-based selection in graph pruning. Moreover, our technique enhances the interpretability of these models. We achieved exceptional results by testing our approach on four distinct datasets, where it simultaneously reduced parameters, improved model interpretability, and maintained or surpassed the original model's performance.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more robust estimator, one that adapts to the most critical elements of prior inputs, has been proposed and shown to successfully overcome this challenge. By analyzing the proposed estimator's performance, we establish that it can successfully identify the top elements of a given vector even if the sketch uses a relatively low number of dimensions, significantly improving upon the count of $\tilde{O}(k^2)$ required by the classic estimator. Moreover, our results demonstrate that this new estimator excels not just in the own-sketch setting but also in settings where the sketch is employed by other users.

Building on previous findings, we discovered that a compact, minimally immersed surface in the space of scalar curvature $R_{can}$ can be expressed as the sum of two components: a conformally asymptotic Ricci-soliton, and a surface with altered conformal structure and removed singularities. This work extends those outcomes to surfaces defined over the complex numbers $\mathbb{C}^2$ with spaces of scalar curvature containing a singularity, resulting in the removal of that singularity.

The Nernst effect is examined in a vortex state of a type-II superconductor with a strong magnetic field, where the Hall conductivity is much larger than the normal conductivity. Calculations are based on a quasiclassical treatment of superconducting electrons in a magnetic field and their interaction with normal electrons. A key finding is that the Nernst coefficient is directly proportional to the transport coefficient of normal electrons in the presence of a strong magnetic field. Another important outcome is that the vortex state enhances the transport coefficient over the normal state, and this enhancement increases with the thickness of the superconductor. Additionally, the entropy of the vortex state is directly proportional to the transport coefficient and shows a similar increase with the thickness of the superconductor.

Optimal resource allocation, a fundamental concept in Operations Research and Management Science, is inherently interconnected with the adaptive capabilities of complex systems. However, the time-consuming computation of optimal policies through direct optimization often hinders their implementation in time-sensitive applications. A commonly employed solution involves the development of feedback policies that balance exploration and exploitation, but these typically overlook the inherent adaptability of systems and often result in suboptimal performance. In contrast, we propose a framework that leverages machine learning to model the time-varying characteristics of systems and integrates this representation into a stochastic optimization framework. Our approach prioritizes the efficient discovery of policies that minimize computation and prediction errors, enabling the rapid adaptation of systems in response to changes, and facilitating the exploration of promising areas in a data-driven manner. We evaluate our method through simulations of energy management systems and find that it yields superior performance compared to conventional approaches in scenarios with rapid changes.

The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning's multiple applications have uncovered several weaknesses, specifically when employed for sequential data forecasting, notably stock price prediction. This research introduces three distinct models using BERT and GAN, which outperform benchmark models according to evaluation criteria. A BERT-Integrated Long Short-Term Memory model and a BERT-Integrated GAN demonstrate superior performance in prediction accuracy and meta-learning objectives. A BERT-Integrated Self-Recurrent GAN exhibits exceptional stock price prediction efficacy, ranking among the top performers in various competitions.

The interactions between compact accretors and their companion stars in binary systems are significantly influenced by the transfer of energy and matter, which in turn depends on the properties of the transferred material, specifically its viscosity and the rate at which it's released. This paper presents a new theoretical framework called SCATTER that accounts for shared envelopes in compact binary systems undergoing transient or persistent accretion. This framework is a revision of the existing formalism by Katagiri et al. (2014), and it is an improvement that includes considerations for the complex processes involving the envelopes of the companion stars. SCATTER is a revised version that includes updated equations for the properties of the envelope, including the calculation of the mass of the accreted material, the rate at which it's released, and the viscosity of the envelope. This revised formula is called R2.5, and it is based on R2 by Tavani (2004), with the addition of the mass of the accreted material. This new formula is a revision of the existing formula by Tavani (2004), and it is an improvement that includes considerations for the complex processes involving the envelopes of the companion stars.

In this research, we examine the potential of future TeV-scale $e^+e^-$ colliders to study double Higgs boson production at the tree level within the framework of the Standard Model and its notable variant theories, such as the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model and those involving extra Higgs doublets. We focus on the impact of BSM Higgs interactions on the double Higgs creation process and identify which of them have a significant effect. We also explore how sensitive this process is to the BSM interactions in the relevant energy range and consider several Effective Field Theory scenarios. We demonstrate that a TeV-scale $e^+e^-$ collider can provide detailed insights into the nature of Higgs boson interactions responsible for their pair creation. Additionally, we show that this process is highly responsive to BSM interactions, with a significant impact that exceeds the square of the BSM contributions by several orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we found that the double Higgs creation process is sensitive to the BSM interactions in the relevant energy range, with a response that is significantly greater than other processes involving Higgs bosons, such as Higgs decays or mono-Higgs boson production in proton-proton collisions. This sensitivity is largely independent of the BSM scenarios, yielding a reliable indicator of new physics in the Higgs sector, even if the BSM interactions differ notably from those predicted by the model we are investigating.

The current formulation of general relativity, described by the Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian, is the foundation for Einstein's theory. However, it was discovered that this formulation is not the most comprehensive or representative form of the theory. Various alternative Lagrangians, which are compatible with the constraints of general relativity, have been proposed over the years. These proposed Lagrangians can lead to distinct implications, including new degrees of freedom potentially emerging below the Einstein gravity scale, which could be observable in high-precision experiments such as the LHC and future gravitational wave detectors. A systematic classification of these alternative Lagrangians, which are known as non-Einstein Lagrangians, has been developed. They can be grouped into three categories: metric modifications, matter modifications, and composite constructions. A review of the known non-Einstein Lagrangians is provided, with a discussion on their potential to be tested in current and future experiments, which include gravitational wave signals, high-precision tests of the gravitational potential, electromagnetic and particle physics, and cosmic microwave background observations.

The problem of localized shocks in $\AdS_5$ interacting with each other is an unsolved issue in the theory of generalized hydrodynamics. A new approach has been discovered that generalizes the hydrodynamical description through a perturbative expansion in the ratio of spatial distances to the length scale of localization. This approach has been confirmed to yield accurate results when compared to numerical solutions for specific sequences of shocks. The discovered approach allows for the description of the interaction of shocks with distinct temperatures, chemical potentials, and velocities. The approach has been found to extend beyond the realm of hydrodynamics, also providing a new view of the interaction between localized operators in $\AdS_5$.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and iron oxide grains, at its interface and perpendicular to its long axis. Our research showed that the drag it exerted varied significantly depending on the direction from which it was measured, a phenomenon known as asymmetry. As the solid's speed increased, the drag it caused also grew, but in a way that differed based on the angle of measurement. When the solid was pulled through the grains at an angle, its frictional resistance followed the pattern of power laws commonly seen in studies of granular materials, but when measured perpendicularly, it conformed to the behavior of fluids. One notable aspect of this research was the discovery of force oscillations that the solid experienced when moved quickly through the grains, a phenomenon that had not been previously reported.

Using observations from the VLT, we've studied a distant starbursting galaxy, finding evidence of massive gas outflows linked to star formation, as they show velocities equivalent to several times the speed of light. With help from dust emission, we've mapped a galactic "snowfall" affecting nearby star formation, and our findings indicate outflows are more pronounced in regions with highest star formation rates. We've also detected molecular gas in excess of what's typically associated with star formation, suggesting the galaxy has sufficient material for multiple generations of star formation. Our data combined with computer simulations reveal outflows may hinder star formation formation by as much as 50% and could be a key factor in galaxies like this one ignoring the established relationship between galaxy mass and formation rate.

High-dimensional Bayesian inference is frequently employed in complex computational models to address real-world challenges, albeit often at the expense of efficiency when dealing with a large number of parameters. To tackle this issue, we developed an organizational framework called BoGraph that enhances Bayesian inference by breaking down the analysis into smaller components, utilizing precomputed statistical patterns derived from historical data to inform the posterior estimation. This approach allows for a reduction in the computational burden by limiting the number of parameters to be estimated simultaneously, thereby speeding up the calculation. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in relation to conventional techniques and examined its practical implications in the context of a high-performance computer simulation of weather patterns, utilizing over 2000 variables in the process.

Our research investigates the triangular flow phenomenon denoted by $\cos(3\delta)\,p_T\,v_3$ as it pertains to particle distribution in three dimensions. We analyzed this phenomenon in two scenarios using the AMPT model: first in a simplified model without initial conditions, and second in a more complex model with initial conditions drawn from a variety of sources. We examined these phenomena in both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Our findings suggest that the source of triangular flow originates from the intrinsic properties of quark and gluon jets. We investigated the role of initial state anisotropy in driving triangular flow by varying the anisotropy degree in 62 GeV Au+Au collisions. Our results demonstrate that the coefficient of triangular flow correlates linearly with initial state anisotropy, and increases with rising anisotropy degree. We also explored contributions from both valence quarks and gluons within the initial state. We found that the valence quark contribution accounts for approximately 55% of the coefficient, while the gluon contribution accounts for around 45%.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, thereby facilitating seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to their poor quality, causing concerns among both researchers and practitioners.  Existing quality assessment approaches for Linked Data, although sound in theory, prove difficult to apply in practice because of their limited scalability and lack of comprehensiveness in measuring quality.  To address these challenges, we propose a scalable and comprehensive approach for evaluating the quality of RDF datasets, taking into consideration both intrinsic and extrinsic quality aspects.  Our approach leverages existing best practices and quality measures, integrating them in an integrated quality framework that incorporates both subjective and objective quality evaluation methods.  To enhance scalability, we design a distributed quality evaluation framework with flexible scalability, enabling it to handle large-scale datasets.  Furthermore, we showcase the effectiveness of our approach by conducting a pilot study on a sample dataset and making our system's source code available for public use.

The precise assessment of parameter uncertainty in numerical solutions to partial differential equations and differential equations is a long-standing issue in scientific computing, particularly when data is collected discretely. A novel approach is presented that enhances the evaluation of parameter uncertainty in discrete data sets, leading to faster and more accurate results. This method, suited for complex systems requiring computational models, is particularly valuable in analyzing deterministic and stochastic processes that are observed with some error, using a statistical model that can handle abnormalities and discrepancies in data. The new approach outperforms existing methods in terms of speed and accuracy, especially in solving differential equations and assessing parameter uncertainty in discrete data sets. The method is applied to a nonlinear diffusion equation with noise, as well as a model of intracellular calcium trafficking that includes noise.

This is the fifth study in a series examining the link between ionization and density within ionized gas layers of nearby Seyfert galaxies. Previous research revealed a previously unknown relationship between ionization and density in these galaxies, along with a distinct distribution of ionization and a sharp cutoff at extremely high ionization levels. The present investigation involves a new, larger sample of 32 Seyfert galaxies observed using the VLT FORS2 spectrograph, along with new data from 7 galaxies previously studied. The detection of a particular emission line at 3727 Angstroms, which is sensitive to both ionization and density, allows for a comparison with similar observations of star-forming galaxies. The resulting data, after controlling for factors like gas ionization, orientation, and contaminating light from surrounding star-forming regions, show a dispersion that is greater than expected. The study also discovers a local maximum in emission at a certain angle to the axis of ionization, which is not fully explained by current models of gas dynamics. It is possible that this peak corresponds to a region of gas in shock due to a supermassive black hole's gravitational field, with a specific velocity vector. If confirmed, this would provide the first observational evidence of shocked gas in the context of a galaxy's host environment.

The speed at which software applications are being developed is accelerating, with decreasing development cycles requiring immediate deployment. This pace creates opportunities for software development to be decentralized and self-sustaining in a manner reminiscent of scientific progress. However, ensuring the quality of continuously evolving software systems poses significant challenges due to the limitations of traditional testing approaches, which are often hampered by slow iteration cycles. Consequently, there's a growing need for more agile and effective testing methodologies that can tackle the complexities of software development in the edge domain. In response to these demands, we're introducing a novel event-focused testing framework, which can be applied to the development of edge applications. This framework utilizes events as a central unifying concept to integrate disparate components and streamline the development process. We've also introduced a set of associated tools to help developers craft high-quality edge applications. Our event-focused testing approach can be used in conjunction with any programming language and framework, making it a versatile solution. To illustrate the efficacy of this approach, we've conducted a case study involving the development of an autonomous video analytics system, which demonstrates that our event-focused testing approach can be up to 5 times more efficient than traditional testing methods.

The ATLAS collaboration has analyzed 80 fb^-1 of LHC data to investigate possible violations of CP symmetry and rare occurrences in beauty mesons decaying to muons. The results for various processes are as follows: The data rejects the standard model prediction for a particular type of CP-violating decay, with an excess ratio of 0.75 ± 0.09 to 0.85 ± 0.11, at a 4.5-sigma confidence level. Additionally, the observed frequency of another type of CP-violating decay exceeds the standard model's prediction at a level of 3.7 sigma. The data also reveals an excess of decays involving a muon and an antineutron in 2.4 sigma excess and an excess of decays involving an electron and an antielectron in 1.4 sigma.

The development and testing of autonomous driving technologies require vast amounts of simulation data, but manually crafting realistic scenes is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. To automate this process, we've developed SceneGen, a technique that uses 3D bounding box representations to efficiently simulate realistic traffic scenarios. SceneGen works by generating a base scene, defining the positions and movements of participating objects within that scene, and finally, it utilizes a series of rules and heuristics to place additional objects within the scene in a way that mimics real-world traffic patterns. To train SceneGen, we've developed a training system that simulates the perspectives of multiple objects within the scene, allowing the system to learn from a significantly reduced amount of data compared to traditional approaches. Our results show that SceneGen is capable of generating high-quality, realistic scenarios that are on par with those created by human operators, and it does so in a fraction of the time.

On a Cayley tree, we define a new set of spin systems based on a novel approach that combines local rules. We show that these systems are closely related to the Ising model and prove the existence of a periodic equilibrium state for a specific set of temperatures and external fields. We also find a non-periodic equilibrium state for another set of parameters and suspect that it may be unique. We discuss how these results relate to a recent phenomenon of bi-periodicity and propose a uniqueness criterion.

A nonlinear problem representing a wide range of conservation laws and involving a non-standard stiff operator is formulated, and a specific application to the compressible Navier-Stokes equations is detailed. A novel approach combining linearization, approximation, and reduction is used to transform the problem into a large linear system characterized by a compact, invertible operator with a non-uniform spectrum. The approach leverages the specific structure of the operator to develop a preconditioned Krylov solver that takes advantage of the operator's properties, resulting in improved convergence rate. The proposed method is particularly useful for solving large systems arising from finite element and finite volume numerical schemes, and its efficiency is demonstrated using the compressible Navier-Stokes equations solved with a finite element method.

A combinatorial approach is taken to demonstrate the ergodicity of a polynomial system associated with a series that meets specific requirements, utilizing a principle derived from theorems involving combinatorial structures known as posets.

We investigated the growth of dust grains in molecular clouds using a multi-zone model, specifically focusing on zones where gas temperatures drop below 800K. This approach enabled us to explore dust development in molecular clouds rich in gas and poor in metal content. Our model showed that in such environments, dust growth is hampered by gas temperature and presence of Ly-alpha photons. However, it also revealed that dust growth accelerates in regions with high gas density and when dust particles are overcoated with organic compounds. This occurred even if metal content remained low. We examined supernovae exploding within these molecular clouds and found that they produce large amounts of dust. This indicates previous studies may have overestimated the importance of dust creation in early galaxies. All-inclusive models, considering dust production in supernovae, suggest the bulk of dust formed in such events is heavy and polycyclic, with the potential to absorb small amounts of light. This has implications for cloud temperature and molecular hydrogen formation. Furthermore, these models imply dust creation in supernovae can lead to significant heating of surrounding gas, potentially making it more accessible for future star formation.

In recent times, there's been significant advancement in 3D object detection, with several challenging datasets being used to test this technology. However, the Far3Det dataset stands out from the crowd due to its unique characteristics - it features extremely distant objects within a 1km range. The 3D detection models tested on this dataset reveal a notable performance drop when compared to models trained and tested on closer ranges. To improve the Far3Det dataset's 3D detection performance, our research indicates that several key issues need to be addressed. These problems include substantial calibration errors, absent depth maps in RGB images, and difficult distant object classifications. To tackle these challenges, our Far3Det framework incorporates a novel approach that utilizes LiDAR data and RGB images in a combined 3D detector design. This detector includes a range-aware range-based regression module that addresses the calibration issues, and a class-agnostic attribute module that tackles the difficult distant object classifications. In our experiments, our research shows that the Far3Det framework is highly effective in enhancing 3D detection performance on the Far3Det dataset. It achieves a mean average precision (MAP) of 33.29%, representing a significant improvement over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

Quantum chemistry systems represented by Hamiltonians can be used to investigate the electronic properties of compounds using two primary methods: the diagonalization technique or quantum dynamics simulations. This work focuses on the former approach, involving the resolution of a second quantization Hamiltonian that describes interacting electrons in a finite space. Our goal is to develop a quantum classical hybrid algorithm, suitable for quantum machine learning implementation, to obtain an approximate ground state of such Hamiltonians. The proposed method leverages quantum unitary operators that rotate the second quantization Fock space and identifies the ground state by measuring the overlap between quantum states. Monte Carlo strategies can be employed to find the optimal parameter values that maximize this overlap, thereby yielding an approximate ground state. This hybrid approach has been tested against established quantum chemistry methods for calculating bond lengths, lattice energies, and potential energy curves in the benchmark systems H$_2$, H$_4$, H$_3$O, HfCl$_4$, H$_2$O, and CH$_2$. Furthermore, we explore the potential of our method to be executed on a quantum-in-the-middle scenario using a quantum processor unit followed by classical numerical integration on a classical device.

Our novel approach achieves non-rigid alignment of a volumetric medical image with a surface-based medical image, both derived from patients with structural heart disease, using a data-driven biomechanical model. This method utilizes a finite element model, guided by computed tomography data and heart wall thickness information, to efficiently and accurately map a 3D volume to a corresponding surface. We validate our technique and a comparison method against a ground truth non-rigid alignment, demonstrating its effectiveness and relatively short computation time. Additionally, we apply our technique to non-rigid registration of MR and CT images, a crucial step in preoperative planning for transapical TAVR.

In a stationary spacetime, the energy-momentum tensor of a spherical distribution of matter is investigated under the assumption of conformal symmetry. It is demonstrated that this tensor's conformal invariance applies universally, unrelated to the symmetry of the matter itself, a requirement being the presence of a conformally invariant potential. It is additionally shown that the celebrated Weinberg's theorem is a specific case of a more broadly applicable conjecture, namely that a linear potential results in a flat spacetime.

Most machine learning models rely on similar data to learn from each other for transfer learning. However, when it comes to estimating scene flow from stereo images, relying on neighbor-based training can be problematic due to the presence of holes in depth maps, causing difficulties in the training process. To overcome this issue, we've developed a metric learning approach that allows for self-supervised scene flow estimation from a single image. The approach involves creating a metric that assesses the similarity between predicted scene flows and actual flows, using a metric that measures the disparity between these two quantities. To prevent the model from relying on neighbor-based training, we've introduced two techniques: first, we've modified the metric's loss function to prioritize the prediction of flow directions over actual disparities; and second, we've developed a filter to eliminate neighbor-based predictions. When tested on the DTLD dataset, our method outperformed existing self-supervised scene flow estimation techniques and achieved comparable results to model fine-tuned with real data. Moreover, we've demonstrated that our approach can be applied to other 3D reconstruction tasks, such as point cloud filtering, by adapting the target object.

In recent years, AI systems, characterized by rapid neural network computations and substantial memory usage, have significantly contributed to the growth of computing power. Nonetheless, the high energy consumption and extensive memory requirements of these systems pose significant challenges for their deployment on mobile devices and edge computing platforms. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that utilizes a type of Random Neural Network, known as the Spiking Random Neural Network. This framework is designed to classify input data into predefined categories by generating random synaptic connections and minimizing energy consumption. We have successfully demonstrated this framework by developing a system that utilizes a Spiking Random Neural Network to deliver a high accuracy of 96.97% in photograph classification using a limited number of neurons. Furthermore, we have observed a marked reduction in energy consumption of up to 90% in our enhanced version.

This research investigates the properties of strange quark matter at high temperature and density, specifically within spin-aligned neutron stars. We used the MIT bag model to create a model of strange quark matter and solved the Einstein-Maxwell-Dirac equations for a spinning strange quark star in the presence of a magnetic field, considering the effects of temperature, density, and magnetic field on the quark star's structure. Our study reveals that temperature, density, and magnetic field all impact the quark star's radius, volume, and gravitational field in notable ways. Conversely, the change in the AdS black hole's temperature and the quark star's rotation period remain unaffected by the magnetic field. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that a magnetic field can trigger a phase transition from a neutron star to a spinning strange quark star star.

Given a finite simple graph G that is cubic, we define a pairing of edges that is ideal, in relation to G, as a set P of edges, satisfying specific conditions, such that the number of edges in a particular subset is always even. Our main objective here is to demonstrate the nonexistence of a pairing of edges that is ideal for any Hamiltonian circuit in a particular category of graphs, and to establish this nonexistence holds universally. Additionally, we show that a particular subset of graphs, obtained by removing the edges of a single color from a cubic graph that is triangulated, does not have a Hamiltonian circuit. Our approach to achieving this involves the concept of edge-tinting in graph theory. Moreover, we establish that a particular subset of these graphs, after being colored using a method we call 'edge-tinting', does not have a Hamiltonian circuit.

Suppose we have a set of parametric univariate polynomials, represented in the variable $x$, where each parameter holds a distinct value from the set $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and there are an infinite number of choices available. If we can establish that a specific quadratic polynomial $f$ contains only irreducible factors with a distinct prime characteristic, specifically $p$, when the parameters are set to a particular value, we can conclude that $f$ is prime when the parameters are set to any value other than that particular value. Additionally, if we can determine that a particular linear polynomial $g$ does not share a common factor with the base field $\mathbb{Z}_p$ when the parameters are set to a particular value, we can conclude that $g$ does not share a common factor with the base field $\mathbb{Z}_p$ when the parameters are set to any value other than that particular value. Containerized microservices offer better security through compartmentalization,
but this isolation depends on accurate configuration of security mechanisms,
such as SELinux and AppArmor. Automating this process is complicated due to the
complexity of policies and raw operating system system calls underlying them.
We've developed a solution called Timeloops, an automated learning algorithm
for defining policies within containers by mapping system calls to temporal logic
formulas, using data from system call histories and runtime logs. This approach
scales efficiently because it focuses only on relevant system calls, learned from
data and not through exploration of all possible system calls, and includes a
working implementation of Timeloops.

Investigating the dark matter sector within the augmented Standard Model of $B-L$ extended to include three right-handed neutrinos, we discover a plausible connection between the dark matter and the Higgs sector. Due to a global $U(1)_B$ symmetry, a pseudo-Goldstone boson is formed, and its connection to the Higgs sector allows it to interact with the standard model in a manner consistent with experimental data. Furthermore, we find that this pseudo-Goldstone dark matter phenomenon is linked to a specific regulatory mechanism required to prevent neutrino instability, and thus, we can relate the dark matter density to the parameters governing neutrino masses. Within the parameter space that aligns with theoretical constraints and meets experimental requirements, we determine that the dark matter density can be explained by selecting an appropriate value for the vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field. Additionally, we identify the threshold below which the pseudo-Goldstone dark matter must reside in order to avoid conflicting with experimental observations of particle physics, and we find the minimum radius of the dark sector by considering the constraints imposed by neutrino physics.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that addresses the challenging problem of tracking complex systems with numerous state variables in a partially observable environment. This implementation is unique as it deviates from the conventional Gaussian assumption often made in advanced Bayesian filters such as the Gaussian mixture (GM) and Gaussian linear models. Instead of relying on Gaussian approximations, this PMBM filter leverages a novel lattice-based approach to correct target state uncertainties, thereby improving its scalability and efficiency. To further enhance its performance, a new method is proposed for updating the target probability density function, enabling it to effectively utilize limited observational data. To validate its effectiveness, the filter is applied to two realistic scenarios: one involving the tracking of a submarine with parameters influencing its motion and another with the detection of targets with varying sizes in clutters, where it demonstrates improved accuracy in its estimations.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an internal non-Lipschitz component, extending the work of Fridman and Tadewi. By first establishing an new bound for the population's minimum value, we then demonstrate the feasibility of controlling the population within a closed interval over a specified time frame. This control is achieved via the application of a targeted removal strategy, supplemented by additional methods including the introduction of a competing species and the manipulation of the population's internal parameters.

The success of soccer teams is often decided by a few pivotal moments in games, specifically situations like set pieces, counter-attacks, and defending a goal. These scenarios have a significant impact on the final score and ultimately the outcome of the game. As such, coaches and teams devote considerable time and effort to planning and executing these critical situations. This motivation behind this study comes from the desire to enhance the effectiveness of teams in these situations through the use of deep reinforcement learning. We created a virtual soccer environment that can simulate game situations and allow agents to learn strategies by experimenting with different actions in different environments, which represents real-game scenarios more accurately than previously attempted. Our approach results in agents developing more practical solutions, as they are able to learn strategies that successfully score goals at a rate of about 0.7 per 100 situations, which is comparable to or better than the success rate of top-level soccer teams in similar scenarios.

High-resolution subsurface imaging through seismic data can be achieved through waveform inversion, a method that uses forward and inverse modeling to generate detailed images of the Earth's properties. However, traditional waveform inversion techniques are hindered by their low-resolution output and expensive computational costs. Two recently developed methods, Frechet derivative inversion and expanded source waveform inversion, offer more accurate results with reduced computational demands, but have limitations in their own right. This study explores the application of expanded source waveform inversion, which breaks down the inverse problem into more manageable parts by gradually increasing the size of synthetic source wavelets to match real data, accompanied by advancements in seismic data preprocessing and preconditioning. Our research utilizes numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in recovering high-resolution velocity models. The study specifically evaluates how the size of expanded source wavelets impacts computational efficiency and image resolution, with promising results showing improved velocity models obtained through expanded source waveform inversion relative to conventional waveform inversion.

We have discovered a novel method of creating optical asymmetry in cylindrical structures coated with dielectric materials by applying quantum compression concepts.  This technique involves the application of classical electromagnetic boundary conditions in a quantum framework, a process that results in the reflection and transmission coefficients becoming non-reciprocal when light travels in these structures at super-luminal speeds.  A corresponding theory has been developed to explain this phenomenon, and we have demonstrated its validity with a numerical model, also outlining the conditions required for the occurrence of optical asymmetry.

The source IGR J19294+1816, an atoll type compact binary system containing a black hole or a neutron star, exhibited significant activity in 2019 with X-ray flare emissions. We analyzed these emissions using the AstroSat satellite, and our data revealed a distinctive mHz QPO and an absorption line at approximately 11.12 keV, which could indicate the presence of a cyclotron harmonic. We observed the mHz QPO to be linked to the source's inner accretion disk, while the higher energy harmonic, at around 22.24 keV, remained undetected. Our findings support the idea that the 11.12 keV line is a cyclotron harmonic, likely related to a magnetic field strength of approximately 319 G. We also found the mHz QPO to be an intrinsic feature of the system's spectral emissions, and our data suggest it is connected to the inner accretion disk. Moreover, we detected the 11.12 keV line to be an harmonic of the 5.56 keV line, and our results indicate the absence of the 22.24 keV line, and we observed the ratio of the harmonic to the base line to be less than two. We also found the 5.56 keV line to originate from the innermost point of the accretion disk, and our data suggest the ratio of the harmonic to the base line to be less than two.

A new model of interaction on a random graph is introduced, taking into account both competitive and colonizing traits in species. This leads to a complex dynamics where the probability of a species' elimination is influenced by the degree of its nearest neighbors. Coexistence, where multiple species coexist, can occur along with the possibility of species elimination. A key feature of this model is the presence of a competition-colonization balance which can result in both stable coexistence and species elimination. A 'frozen lake' effect is observed, where species coexist if the model starts with two species, but this does not hold true for a larger number of species. A key innovation of this model involves an algorithm that generates highly connected subgraphs, allowing it to capture the dynamics of species elimination and coexistence in a more realistic way. A competition-colonization balance can lead to species coexistence, and it has been shown that it is possible for a species to become extinct due to the influence of its own members. A distinction is made between a model that generates random graphs and one that generates highly connected subgraphs, and it is shown that the latter can result in a 'ferromagnetic' state where all species eventually become extinct except for the one that was present at the beginning.
